newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan ruling party to invest in Ishigaki, Japan.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan ruling party to invest in Ishigaki, Japan.

text.p: Taiwan's ruling party said on Tuesday it would invest in the tourism industry in Japan's southern island of Ishigaki, but was losing hope on plans to turn it into a transshipment centre for trade with China.
The Nationalist Party urged the Japanese government to deregulate its investment restrictions and allow Okinawa and Ishigaki islands to become free-trade zones.
"The investment plan's focus is on the tourism development (of Ishigaki)," a ruling party management committee spokeswoman said by telephone.
She declined to confirm a report by the Economic Daily News that her party's investment would total US$200 million.
The spokeswoman said U.S. military bases on Okinawa and Ishigaki provide sound infrastructure beneficial for business development on both islands.

But while sanguine on Ishigaki's prospect for tourism, Nationalist business leader Liu Tai-ying told the newspaper that it was "less likely" the island could be transformed into a transshipment centre, as the party previously had hoped.
Liu did not say why his party was giving up on the transshipment scheme.

Despite diminishing hopes for the transshipment centre, another Nationalist Party business leader, Central Investment Holding chairman Yang Tsung-tse, said his party's tourism investment plan "is not empty talk".
"The party will invest in tourism development, shopping malls and hotels," Yang was quoted by the Economic Daily News as saying.

In a sign that private enterprises also are eager to capture new businesses in Ishigaki, Taiwan's TransAsia Airways said on Tuesday it might begin flights to Ishigaki, although no firm schedule has been set.

Transshipment centres act as essential liaisons for Taiwan's huge business flows to China, where Taipei has banned direct transport, communications and other official links for nearly five decades on political grounds.

Hong Kong remains the chief transshipment centre for cargoes moving between Taiwan and China, but Taiwan is actively hunting for possible alternatives ahead of the British colony's mid-1997 handover to Beijing rule.
Taipei fears China could exploit Taiwan's reliance on Hong Kong for political concessions after Beijing takes control of the territory in July.

Taipei also faces mounting pressure from Taiwan firms that operate on the mainland to ease the restrictions on direct links. Some 25,000 Taiwan firms have poured US$20 billion into China since indirect economic ties began to blossom a decade ago.
Ishigaki lies just 150 miles (240 km) east of Taiwan's northern Keelung port and can be reached from Taipei in 35 minutes by air. It is located just west of Japan's southern major island of Okinawa.
